How to design a business card that works: 13 rules

A business card is small, so every millimetre has a job. These are the rules we use when we lay out cards for GTA businesses — and the mistakes we see most often on files sent to print.

By the Satin Graphic teamUpdated October 10, 2026
On this pageWhy the card still mattersContent: decide what the card must doLayout: give it roomType and colourPaper, finishes and productionQuick checklist before you orderNo designer? No problemQuestionsRelatedBusiness cardsDesign servicesArtwork guidelines

Why the card still matters

A business card is usually the first printed piece of a brand that someone holds in their hand, and it is often the one they keep in a wallet, a cardholder or a pile on a desk. It is also the cheapest piece of marketing you will buy: at our shop, 500 regular 14 pt matte cards start at $26 before tax. Because it is so inexpensive, the difference between a card that works and one that gets thrown out comes down almost entirely to design and paper — not budget.

The thirteen rules below are grouped into content, layout, type and colour, and production. Follow them and the card will read clearly, look professional and print without surprises.

Content: decide what the card must do

1. Start with one job. Decide what you want the person to do after meeting you — call, book online, visit the shop, follow you on Instagram — and make that the most visible contact detail. Everything else supports it.

2. Include only what someone will use. For most local businesses that is: your name, title, business name and logo, one phone number, one email, the website, and the address if customers visit you. Fax numbers, three phone lines and every social handle you own make the card harder to read.

3. Say what you do. A logo and a name are not always enough — “Acme Group” could be anything. Add a short line such as “Residential HVAC · Vaughan & York Region” or “Custom kitchen cabinetry · Woodbridge”. A clear line of service turns a card into a reminder of why someone should call.

4. Use the back. Printing both sides adds only $6 to an order at our shop, and it doubles the space. Put the logo and tagline on one side and the contact details on the other, or use the back for a short list of services, a map pin, opening hours or a QR code to your booking page or reviews.

Layout: give it room

5. Respect the trim, bleed and safe area. A standard North American card is 3.5 × 2 in. Build the file at 3.75 × 2.25 in so that colour and images run 0.125 in (3 mm) past every edge — the bleed — and keep text and logos at least 0.125 in inside the trim line. Cutting machines are precise but not perfect, and anything right on the edge can be trimmed off or look off-centre.

6. Leave white space. Crowded cards look cheap. Group related information (name and title; phone, email and web) and leave clear space between groups. Aligning everything to one or two edges usually looks better than centring every line.

7. Make the hierarchy obvious. The eye should land on the name or logo first, then the main contact method, then the rest. Achieve that with size and weight, not with five different colours.

Type and colour

8. Keep fonts readable at small sizes. Use no more than two typefaces. Body text below about 7 pt becomes hard to read, especially for older customers, and very thin or script fonts break up in print. Phone numbers and emails deserve a clean, simple font.

9. Work in CMYK and use proper black. Screens show RGB colour; presses print CMYK. Bright RGB blues, greens and oranges shift when converted, so design in CMYK from the start and give us Pantone references for brand colours. Small text should be 100% black (K only) so it stays sharp; large solid black areas look richer in rich black (C60 M40 Y40 K100).

10. Use high contrast. Light grey text on white, or dark blue on black, looks elegant on a monitor and disappears on paper. If in doubt, increase the contrast.

Paper, finishes and production

11. Choose the stock for the impression you want. Our regular cards are 14 pt matte — practical, easy to write on and good for most trades and service businesses. Luxury cards are 16 pt with a soft-touch finish, which is slightly thicker and has a velvety feel in the hand; 500 start at $34.50. Matte and soft-touch surfaces reduce glare and fingerprints. If you want to write appointment times on the card, avoid high-gloss coatings.

12. Use special touches with purpose. Rounded corners ($4 extra on our configurator) feel softer and suit wellness, beauty and family-oriented brands; square corners read as classic and corporate. Whatever you choose, use it consistently with your other printed pieces.

13. Send a print-ready file and approve the proof. Export a PDF (PDF/X-1a or “High Quality Print”) at 300 DPI with crop marks and bleed, fonts outlined or embedded, and images embedded. Single pages, not spreads. We send a digital proof before anything goes to press — read every digit of the phone number and email aloud before you approve it. Typos on cards are the single most common reprint we see.

Quick checklist before you order

CheckSpec
Trim size3.5 × 2 in
Document size with bleed3.75 × 2.25 in (0.125 in bleed each side)
Safe areaText and logos 0.125 in inside the trim
Resolution300 DPI at final size
ColourCMYK; small text 100% K; large blacks C60 M40 Y40 K100
FilePrint-ready PDF; AI, EPS, packaged INDD, TIFF or PSD also accepted
FontsOutlined or embedded

Standard production is 7–10 business days after proof approval. If you need cards for a specific event, tell us the date when you order and we’ll confirm what’s possible.

No designer? No problem

If you have a logo but no layout, choose the design option on the business cards page ($100) and our team will set it up from your logo and details, then send a proof. If you don’t have a logo yet, start with our design services. Planning a matching set? Questions

What size is a standard business card in Canada?
3.5 × 2 inches, the same as the US standard. Build the file at 3.75 × 2.25 inches to include a 0.125-inch bleed on every side.
What should be on a business card?
Your name and title, business name and logo, one phone number, one email, your website, the address if customers visit you, and a short line that says what you do. Use the back for services, hours or a QR code.
What paper thickness is best for business cards?
Our regular cards are 14 pt matte, which feels solid and is easy to write on. For a more premium feel, choose our 16 pt soft-touch luxury cards.
Should I put a QR code on my business card?
If it leads somewhere useful — booking, reviews or a portfolio — yes. Print it at least about 0.75 in square with a quiet margin around it, and test it on the proof.
How long does business card printing take?
Standard production at our shop is 7–10 business days after you approve the proof and pay.
